idea.idea: Why 80% of businesses see zero profit from AI.
idea.angle: Stop buying subscriptions and start building operational foundations instead.
idea.audience_problem: Owners feel AI is a magic pill, but they are just bleeding subscription costs.

hooks: Stop buying AI tools until your daily workflows are clean
Buying AI subscriptions won't fix messy daily operations
Why AI tools fail on disorganized business ledgers
piece.hook_reason: It speaks directly to Indian business owners who purchase software tools hoping to fix daily back-office chaos, framing the operational fix accurately.

slides.title: Stop buying AI tools until your daily workflows are clean
slides.subtitle: Automating an unorganized daily routine only creates expensive confusion faster.

slides.myth: Adding AI tools will automatically clean up our back-office daily disorganization.
slides.fact: Automating a messy process simply gets you the mess faster. AI requires clean operational data you can trust.

slides.title: Growth bottlenecks are mostly internal
slides.body: Bain research shows 85% of growth barriers are internal. When WhatsApp order notes, quotations, and Tally registers disagree, software will not solve the operational bottleneck.

slides.title: Fix the foundation first
items: Enforce one single template for incoming customer orders
Reconcile pending dispatch entries with ledgers daily
Define clear discount limits before letting software process billing

slides.quote: Automate a messy process and you simply get the mess faster.

slides.title: How disciplined teams manage AI spend
items: Median firms spend just 12 to 15 dollars per employee monthly
Set strict usage budgets before giving staff tool access
Route simple yes-or-no queries to cheaper light models

piece.caption: How to fix your daily business operations before buying AI software tools. Say you run a building materials counter or a small fabrication shop. If price lists live in staff memory and orders sit across three separate WhatsApp chats, putting AI on top will only send bad quotations out faster. Data from Ramp shows median companies spend only $12 to $15 per worker per month on AI by enforcing budgets and using light models for simple tasks. Before paying for monthly tool licenses, ensure your purchase register and quotation steps follow a clean, written routine. Which daily process in your shop currently breaks whenever order volume doubles?

[5] TechCrunch AI — Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO

Image Credits: Stripe at Stripe Sessions AI Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO Rebecca Bellan 7:54 AM PST · November 6, 2026 Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.
A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.
“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”
Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.
“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”
“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.
October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.
Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.
“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.
Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition.
“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp.
“For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.”
The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty.
“As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.”
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”
tokens go brrr costs go ahhh pic.twitter.com/1whCWCJCyM
“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”
Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.
Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.
Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI , SpaceXAI , and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct . Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.
“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”

[84] YourStory — Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth
URL: https://yourstory.com/2026/10/why-operational-excellence-will-define-the-next-phase-indias-startup-growth
Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth | YourStory Growth rarely announces itself. It arrives as a signed term sheet on a Friday evening, a large client wanting to go live in three weeks, or an investor doubling a commitment.
But the win is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the Monday after.
That Monday tells you whether you have built a company or simply had a good quarter.
When operations become a competitive advantage
In most startups, operations sit in the back seat. It is the team that asks for approvals, slows down contracts, and says “not yet” when sales say “yes”. Founders tolerate it the way one tolerates a seatbelt.
I have never accepted that framing. Bain & Company’s long-running research on growth found that 85% of the barriers to profitable growth are internal, with revenue outgrowing talent at the top of the list. Companies rarely lose to the market. They lose to their own machinery, and that machinery is operations.
Early on, operations feel optional. A small team, a founder who knows everything, a spreadsheet that works. Why design controls for a business that fits in one room?
Because by the time you feel the need, you are already late. Operations built in the middle of a growth spurt is built under pressure: rushed hires, patched processes, controls bolted on after something breaks. Worse, it takes bandwidth from growth itself. The team that should be closing the next client is busy repairing the last one. You slow down precisely when you meant to accelerate.
Nobody lays the tracks after the train has left the station.
This is not a case for bloat. It is a case for sequencing. Build the backbone one stage ahead of where you are, lean and proportionate, so the organisation absorbs growth instead of buckling under it.
The companies that scale most smoothly are rarely the ones scrambling when growth arrives; the reporting, controls and people for the next stage are already in place. Investors notice the difference.
In due diligence, a clean data room and a well-documented control environment often say more about a company's readiness than its growth curve does.
Operations is also where a company's data lives, or should. Every onboarding, approval, and report generates information. Most startups treat it as exhaust. The better ones treat it as instrumentation. When operations own clean, consistent data, leadership stops arguing about whose number is right and starts debating what to do about it. You see a bottleneck forming before a client complains. And automation and AI, which nearly every board is now asking about, only work on data you can trust.
Automate a messy process and you simply get the mess faster.
If your founders and your operations team are looking at different numbers, you do not have a data problem. You have an operations problem.
The same discipline applies to mistakes. A mistake made once is a lesson; made twice, it is a choice.
Every error in a growing firm should leave something behind, whether a changed control, a clearer owner, or a better checklist.
The corollary matters as much. If the same method keeps producing the same disappointing result, the problem is rarely effort. It is the method. Operations should be the function that notices, asks why, and has the licence to change how the work gets done. Processes are not scripture. They are hypotheses, and good operators keep testing them.
Bring operations in before growth is sold, not after
For founders and boards redrawing their organisation charts this year, one test is telling. Do operations hear about a new product, market, or client after it is sold, or while it is being designed? If it is after, operations will always be firefighting, and firefighters rarely get to build anything.
Put operations where growth is planned, not at the end of the line where growth is processed. Give it a seat in strategy reviews, a voice in pricing and launches, and a mandate to say "here is how", not just "not yet".
Three questions are worth asking every quarter:
● If our business doubled next quarter, what would break first?
● Which decisions still need the founder, and should they?
● Would our records survive an investor's due diligence this week?
Will your growth last, or was it just a good quarter?
There is an old military line: amateurs talk strategy, professionals talk logistics.
India's startup story so far has been told in the language of strategy: rounds, valuations, category creation. The next chapter will be about sustaining growth rather than merely achieving it, and it will be told in the language of execution and governance. Momentary growth is an event. Sustained growth is a capability. And capability, in the end, is what operations builds.
(Sandesha Jaitapkar is the COO at Artha Group)
